title: What is known about 1RB0RE_1LC0RD_1LD0LD_1RA0LC_1RA1RF_1RA---
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0RE_1LC0RD_1LD0LD_1RA0LC_1RA1RF_1RA---.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. The machine is a binary counter whose digits are pairs of blocks of 10s. One sweep adds one to it, with an exact rule and an exact step count. That rule is checked against the machine on 24,787 sweeps, and its first two cases are proved in Lean for every size. Rare merge and end events change the list of digits, and they are only partly described.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (F1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 87,460 cells have been visited and 43,726 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Shift rules of the sweep
claims.text: For every n and any tape around: states A and E cross blocks of 10/01 to the right, shifting them by one cell, and C and D cross them to the left unchanged.

claims.title: The first two cases of the tick
claims.text: The whole sweep when the first digit is 0 (tick_stop, 4a + 10 steps) and when the carry passes one digit (tick_pass1, 4a + 8b + 4c + 34 steps). Both hold for every block length and any tape to the right.

claims.title: One sweep is a binary increment
claims.text: At each left turn the tape is 0^inf D> 0 (10)^a followed by digits s (10)^b 1 (10)^c, where the separator s is 0 for a 1 and 0 0 0 for a 0. A sweep turns the leading 1s into 0s (each loses one 10 from c), turns the first 0 into a 1 (it gains one 10 in b), and adds one to a. It takes exactly 6 + 4a + 8Σb + 4Σc + 8n steps over the n digits passed. This holds for 24,787 of the 25,117 sweeps in the first 3·108 steps. The rest are the merge and end events.

claims.title: A list of blocks with carries
claims.text: The events: when the carry passes a digit whose c is 1 and the next digit is 0, the two digits merge into one digit 0, (10)^(b+b'+2) 1 (10)^c' (22 of 25 cases). When the carry passes every digit, the first block is cut off and becomes a new digit. Read off the simulation; the remaining cases are not yet described.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. The block dynamics has not been reduced to a rule.

claims.title: Related holdouts
claims.text: The same table as 1RB0LC_1RC0RC_1LD0RB_1LA0LE_1LD1LF_1LD--- up to renaming and mirroring, started in another state; no common configuration in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps of each.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. The tape of this machine is a long list of blocks of 10s with short separators. The head crosses the whole list on every sweep. On the way the first block grows, and single units of length pass from one block to the next, a little like carries in a counter.

facts.text: Each sweep adds one to a binary counter written in block lengths, with an exact step count.
No halt in the C simulator; 87,460 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
Shift rules for the head crossing blocks, proved in Lean.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.564). Right of the start it stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half).
After 109 steps the tape spans 87,460 cells (66,877 left of the start, 85 right), with a density of 1s of 0.5.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: A list of blocks
html: Three million steps in, the tape reads D> 0 (10)^129 0 (10)^191 1 (10)^255 0 0 0 (10)^158 1 (10)^159 …. The head crosses each block in a fixed number of steps per pair; those crossings are proved in Lean.

Over consecutive sweeps the first block grows by one. Separators flip between 0 and 0 0 0. The blocks on either side of a separator trade single units, so 191 and 255 become 192 and 254, then 193 and 253. How these changes add up over many sweeps is the open part.

sections.heading: A binary counter in block lengths
html: Between the blocks of 10s sit separators: a single 0 or a triple 0 0 0. Read the blocks in pairs joined by a 1, and the separator before each pair as a binary digit: 0 means 1 and 0 0 0 means 0. Each sweep adds one to this number, from the left. Every leading 1 becomes 0 and the first 0 becomes 1, exactly like counting in binary. The head only goes as far as the carry before turning back.

The digits also keep a tally. Each time a digit goes from 0 to 1, its first block grows by one 10; each time it goes from 1 to 0, its second block shrinks by one. When a second block runs out, the digit merges with its neighbour. When the carry runs off the end, the first block of the tape is cut off and becomes a new digit. Those rare events are where a halt could hide, and they are not yet fully described.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machine below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in the other, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

summary: A binary counter whose digits are pairs of 10-blocks, ticked once per sweep by an exact increment rule (checked on 24,787 sweeps, its first cases proved in Lean); rare merge and end events change the digit list.
